newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada says inflation may drop below 1 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada says inflation may drop below 1 pct.

text.p: Bank of Canada governor Gordon Thiessen said on Wednesday that a risk exists that the inflation rate could fall below 1.0 percent, but added that such a fall would be a temporary and unimportant blip.

"Certainly there is a risk that inflation could drop below the 1.0 percent. I don't think it's a risk that it would stay there for very long," Thiessen told reporters after addressing the Toronto Board of Trade.
"Just as in 1995, there was a risk that we were going to go above 3.0 percent because of the effects of the exchange rate depreciation," he added.
Thiessen said one always must focus on the trend rather than on any short-term moves in inflation.

"If it looks like the trend is going up through the top of the band or the trend is going through the bottom of the band, then it seems to me the central bank has got a strong obligation to work hard to resist that," he said.

"But if it's going to be something temporary, then I don't regard that as terribly important as long as we are satisfied that we have got monetary conditions easy enough that the economy is going to pick up in such a way that inflation won't stay below that band," he added.
Thiessen also told reporters that Canadian foreign reserves are at very low levels by global standards.

"Those are essentially government decisions. But I think there is no question that the reserves have gotten very low. And I think it's just good, prudent management to have substantial reserves," Thiessen told reporters.
"Canadian reserves still look low by international standards," he added.

Thiessen said recent improvements in Canada's economic fundamentals means the Bank of Canada now has more latitude to set interest rates independent of moves in U.S. interest rates. Thiessen cautioned no country could avoid the impact of a U.S. rate hike, but said Canada is in a better position to withstand it than it has been in recent years.
"We've got a lot more room to maneuver in the face of that," said Thiessen.

The central bank governor said it is too early to comment on whether its 1.0-3.0 percent target bank for the inflation rate should be lowered in the future. The current target runs until the end of 1998.
"I think at this stage we have to be absolutely agnostic," said Thiessen. "It think it's far too early to make a judgement."
